district-of-columbia._source: Rates are the District's schedule of seven brackets, 4% to 10.75%, with the same thresholds for every filing status, set by D.C. Code 47-1806.03(a)(11). The District does not use the federal standard deduction. It sets its own basic standard deduction: $15,000 for a single filer or married filing separately, $22,500 for head of household, and $30,000 for a married couple filing jointly, at D.C. Code 47-1801.04(3A). Those amounts apply to tax years 2025 and 2026. The law adds a yearly cost-of-living adjustment measured from a 2025 base year, so the first increase can come in 2027. Filers aged 65 or older or blind may claim an additional standard deduction, which this calculator does not include. LEGAL STATUS, as of 2026-10-02: these amounts were first enacted by the D.C. Income and Franchise Tax Conformity and Revision Emergency Amendment Act of 2025 (D.C. Act 26-214, December 3, 2025) and then by the D.C. Income and Franchise Tax Conformity and Revision Temporary Amendment Act of 2025 (D.C. Law 26-89, effective 2026-02-12), which Congress disapproved by H.J. Res. 142, signed 2026-02-18 as Public Law 119-78, and which expired on 2026-09-25. The D.C. Code, current through Sept. 26, 2026, no longer carries paragraph (3A), so its codified text points to the federal section 63(c) amount. The same paragraph (3A), for tax years 2025 through 2029, is re-enacted by Subtitle VII-I, the Tax Code Conformity and Clarification Amendment Act of 2026, in two acts: the Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Support Emergency Act of 2026 (D.C. Act 26-416, effective 2026-08-13, expires 2026-11-11) and the permanent Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Support Act of 2026 (D.C. Act 26-418, transmitted to Congress 2026-08-20, projected law date 2026-11-20). Public Law 119-78 names only the 2025 temporary act, and no resolution disapproving D.C. Act 26-418 had been introduced as of 2026-10-02. The Office of Tax and Revenue's 2026 Form D-40ES, revised March 2026 before either act, lists the federal amounts of $16,100, $24,150 and $32,200. The District sets its own standard deduction and does not follow the federal amount. For 2026 it is $15,000 single, $30,000 married filing jointly and $22,500 head of household, the same as 2025, because DC's yearly inflation increase does not start until 2027.

These amounts first came from short-term DC laws passed in late 2025, the last of which ended on September 25, 2026. For 2026 the same amounts are now set by an emergency DC law in effect until November 11, 2026, and by the District's 2027 budget law, which Congress is reviewing and which is expected to take effect around November 20, 2026.

Congress voted in February 2026 to undo the earlier temporary law and could vote to block the budget law too. If it does, DC would likely switch to the federal amounts: $16,100 single, $32,200 married filing jointly, $24,150 head of household. The District's 2026 estimated-tax form, printed in March before the Council passed the budget law, already shows those federal amounts.

vermont._source: Vermont tax year 2026. BRACKETS for all three filing statuses this page models come from the Vermont Legislative Joint Fiscal Office 2026 Fiscal Facts booklet (issued February 2026), the table on page 50 headed 2026 VERMONT Personal Income Tax Rates and Brackets. Check you are on page 50, because page 49 shows the federal brackets. The four rates are 3.35%, 6.60%, 7.60% and 8.75%, and the table gives single 50,750 / 122,850 / 256,300, married filing jointly 84,700 / 204,750 / 312,050, and head of household 68,000 / 175,500 / 284,150. It also lists married filing separately, which this page does not model. Fiscal Facts is the Legislature's reference publication of current law, not a Department of Taxes schedule: 32 V.S.A. 5822(b)(2) assigns the annual inflation adjustment to the Commissioner of Taxes. https://ljfo.vermont.gov/assets/Publications/2026-Fiscal-Facts-Booklet/Fiscal-Facts-2026.pdf It is not the only official Vermont document carrying these brackets, and it is not the primary one. The Department of Taxes prints the same schedules itself in its 2026 Form IN-114 Instructions (Rev. 10/25), on the SECOND page of that two-page PDF, under the heading 2026 Preliminary Vermont Tax Rates: Schedule X single 50,750 / 122,850 / 256,300, Schedule Y-1 married filing jointly 84,700 / 204,750 / 312,050, Schedule Y-2 married filing separately 42,350 / 102,375 / 156,025, and Schedule Z head of household 68,000 / 175,500 / 284,150, at the same four rates. The Department labels that table Preliminary. The printed header on that page reads Page 1 of 2, so go by the PDF page count, not the header. IN-114 is the departmental authority for the bracket figures on this page and Fiscal Facts corroborates it; the two agree on every threshold. https://tax.vermont.gov/sites/tax/files/documents/IN-114-Instr-2026.pdf STANDARD DEDUCTION figures are Vermont's tax year 2025 amounts, $7,650 single, $15,300 married filing jointly and $11,450 head of household, from the Vermont Department of Taxes 2025 Income Tax Return Booklet, the Form IN-111 Line 4 standard deduction chart. https://tax.vermont.gov/sites/tax/files/documents/Income-Booklet-2025.pdf WHY TWO YEARS: the Department of Taxes has not published a 2026 standard deduction anywhere, including in the IN-114 instructions cited above, which carry rate schedules only. Its 2026 rate schedules exist only as the Preliminary ones in those instructions; the newest schedules on its rate schedules page are still tax year 2025. https://tax.vermont.gov/individuals/personal-income-tax/rates Vermont has published 2026 WITHHOLDING material (GB-1210-2026, RateSched-2026, TaxTables-2026), but those are employer withholding charts covering single and married only, with no head of household column, and their thresholds are not the bracket thresholds, so they are deliberately not cited for any figure on this page. PERSONAL EXEMPTION FOLDED IN 2026-10-03: the same 2025 booklet, Form IN-111 line 5e, reads 'Vermont Personal Exemption Deduction. Multiply Line 5d by $5,300', with no phase-out. The standard deduction field now carries the 2025 standard deduction plus the 2025 exemption: 7,650 + 5,300 = 12,950 single, 15,300 + 10,600 = 25,900 married filing jointly, 11,450 + 5,300 = 16,750 head of household. The only 2026 figure published is the $5,400 withholding allowance in GB-1210-2026, which is a withholding figure, so it is not used. CHILD CARE CONTRIBUTION added 2026-10-03: 32 V.S.A. 10553 (2023 Act 76, section 24, effective July 1, 2024) sets 'The contribution rate shall be 0.44 percent of each employee's covered wages' and lets the employer 'deduct and withhold ... not more than one quarter of the contribution' from the employee; the Department's Child Care Contribution page says 'The maximum an employer may elect to withhold is 0.11% of an employee's wages'. Modelled at that maximum, as Maine, Minnesota, Colorado and Massachusetts are. https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/32/246/10553 ; https://tax.vermont.gov/business/child-care-contribution

texas._source: Texas has no individual income tax. Article VIII, Section 24-a of the Texas Constitution bars the legislature from taxing the net incomes of individuals. https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/CN/htm/CN.8/CN.8.24-a.htm

_noTaxBasis.heading: Why Texas cannot introduce an income tax without amending its constitution
paragraphs: Texas does not merely decline to tax wages; it is constitutionally barred from doing so. Article VIII, Section 24-a of the Texas Constitution provides that the legislature "may not impose a tax on the net incomes of individuals, including an individual's share of partnership and unincorporated association income." Voters added that section on 5 November 2019 through Proposition 4, which also repealed the older Section 24 it replaced.

The difference matters to anyone planning more than a year ahead. Under the old Section 24, an income tax was an ordinary legislative act with a high bar: a majority in both chambers, then approval at a statewide referendum. Since Proposition 4 it is not a legislative question at all. Introducing one would require amending the constitution itself, which takes two-thirds of both the Texas House and the Texas Senate and then a statewide vote. This line on a Texas pay stub is about as fixed as a tax rule gets.

There is also no city or county income tax anywhere in Texas, so the federal figures on this page are the whole withholding picture for a salaried employee. The state funds itself largely through sales tax and local property tax, neither of which is deducted from a paycheck.

florida._source: Florida levies no state individual income tax (Florida Dept. of Revenue). https://floridarevenue.com/

_noTaxBasis.heading: Florida's zero is the output of a formula, not a flat ban
paragraphs: Florida's constitution does not simply forbid taxing individual income. Article VII, Section 5(a) provides that no tax "upon the income of natural persons who are residents or citizens of the state shall be levied by the state, or under its authority, in excess of the aggregate of amounts which may be allowed to be credited upon or deducted from any similar tax levied by the United States or any state."

Read closely, that is a ceiling pegged to federal law rather than a prohibition. Florida may tax personal income up to whatever amount federal law would let a taxpayer credit or deduct against it. No such federal credit for a state income tax exists, so the ceiling computes to zero and Florida withholds nothing from wages. The practical result matches a ban, but the mechanism differs: Florida's zero is the output of a calculation whose other input is written in Washington rather than Tallahassee.
For a 2026 paycheck none of that changes the numbers. Every dollar withheld from a Florida salary on this ladder is federal, and no county or municipality in the state levies an income tax on top.

_noTaxBasis.heading: Nevada has a payroll tax, and it never reaches your pay stub
paragraphs: Nevada levies no individual income tax, but it is not a state without a payroll tax. The Modified Business Tax, imposed under NRS 363B.110, is charged on wages. The reason it never appears among the figures on this page is that the employer owes it, not the employee.

The Nevada Department of Taxation states the rule directly: every employer subject to the state's unemployment compensation law "is also subject to the Modified Business Tax on total gross wages less employee health care benefits paid by the employer." The general business rate has been 1.17% since 1 July 2023, reduced from 1.378%, and the first $50,000 of wages in a quarter is exempt.

For a salaried employee the practical effect is that a Nevada employer's true cost of employing you runs above your gross salary by more than the federal employer-side FICA alone. None of it is deducted from you, and every dollar withheld on this ladder is federal.

tennessee._source: Tennessee has no tax on wages. The Hall income tax, which taxed only interest and dividends, was repealed for tax periods beginning on or after January 1, 2021 (Tennessee Department of Revenue). https://www.tn.gov/revenue/taxes/hall-income-tax.html

_sourceTitles.https://www.tn.gov/revenue/taxes/hall-in: Tennessee Department of Revenue: Hall income tax

_noTaxBasis.heading: Tennessee taxed investment income until 2021, and does not tax wages
paragraphs: Tennessee shed an income tax more recently than most people assume, and the one it shed never touched a paycheck. The Hall income tax, enacted in 1929, was imposed only on individuals and other entities "receiving interest from bonds and notes and dividends from stock." Salary and wages sat outside it from the beginning.

The Tennessee Department of Revenue records that the Hall tax "was repealed for tax periods that begin on January 1, 2021, or later," and instructs taxpayers not to file a return for any year beginning on or after that date. So a Tennessee wage earner's withholding has looked like this ladder for decades, while a Tennessee investor's position changed materially only in 2021.

The distinction still trips up anyone reading older guidance. An article written before 2021 that describes Tennessee as having "an income tax" is talking about interest and dividends, not employment income. The Hall tax never put a state line on a Tennessee pay stub, and nothing has taken its place.

south-dakota.name: South Dakota
south-dakota._source: South Dakota levies no state individual income tax (SD Dept. of Revenue). https://dor.sd.gov/

_noTaxBasis.heading: South Dakota's constitution allows an income tax, then sets a two-thirds bar
paragraphs: South Dakota's constitution does not forbid a tax on wages; it expressly allows one. Article XI, Section 2 provides that "the Legislature is empowered to impose taxes upon incomes and occupations," and that "taxes upon incomes may be graduated and progressive and reasonable exemptions may be provided." The absence of a wage tax in South Dakota is a policy the legislature keeps, not a door the constitution has closed.

What stands in the way is a vote threshold. Section 14, approved by voters on 5 November 1996, provides that "no new tax may be imposed by the State of South Dakota unless by consent of the people by exercise of their right of initiative or by two-thirds vote of all the members elect of each branch of the Legislature." A tax on wages would be a new tax, so it would need either a statewide initiative or two-thirds of all the elected members of both the House and the Senate.

An older clause adds a second lock. Section 13, approved on 7 November 1978, applies the same initiative-or-two-thirds rule to any increase in "the rate of taxation imposed by the state of South Dakota on personal or corporate income or on sales or services." So an income tax would meet the bar once to be created and again each time its rate rose. None of this reaches a paycheck today: South Dakota withholds nothing for the state from any salary on this ladder.

wyoming.name: Wyoming
wyoming._source: Wyoming levies no state individual income tax (WY Dept. of Revenue). https://revenue.wyo.gov/

_noTaxBasis.heading: Wyoming's constitution would make any income tax credit back your sales and property taxes
paragraphs: Wyoming levies no income tax on wages, and its constitution does not ban one outright. It attaches a condition instead. Article 15, Section 18 provides that "no tax shall be imposed upon income without allowing full credit against such tax liability for all sales, use, and ad valorem taxes paid in the taxable year by the same taxpayer to any taxing authority in Wyoming." Voters ratified it at the general election of 5 November 1974.

That is a credit rather than a prohibition. Any future Wyoming income tax would be reduced, dollar for dollar, by the sales tax, use tax and ad valorem taxes such as property tax that the same person had already paid that year to the state or to any local taxing authority in Wyoming. The legislature keeps the power to enact one; the constitution settles in advance that it could collect only what a household owes beyond the taxes it already pays on its purchases and its property.

Section 19, first ratified at that same 1974 election, directs the legislature to levy a 1.5% excise tax on the value of coal, petroleum, natural gas, oil shale and other designated minerals extracted in the state, paid into the Permanent Wyoming Mineral Trust Fund. The constitution declares that the fund "shall remain inviolate" and sends its investment income to the general fund each year. None of it is taken from wages, so the only deductions on a Wyoming pay stub on this ladder are the federal ones.

sources.title: Wyoming Constitution, Article 15, Sections 18 and 19 (Wyoming Secretary of State)

_noTaxBasis.heading: Alaska repealed its income tax in 1980, retroactively, after a court struck down its exemptions
paragraphs: Alaska once withheld income tax from paychecks, and the way it stopped is unusual. Earlier in 1980 the legislature had given most individual taxpayers complete or substantial relief through exemptions based on the number of years each had reported Alaska income. On 4 September 1980 the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that those exemptions violated the equal protection clause of article I, section 1 of the Alaska Constitution. As the legislature put it in its own findings, "the effect of that decision is to reimpose the full income tax burden on all taxpayers."

The legislature chose to remove the tax rather than repair the exemptions. Chapter 2 of the 1980 Second Special Session Laws of Alaska, approved by the governor on 24 September 1980, repealed "the Alaska net income tax on individuals and fiduciaries" retroactive to 1 January 1979, and entitled individuals to a refund of the Alaska income tax paid or withheld for 1979.

The 1980 act did not repeal the chapter that imposed the tax. AS 43.20 is still in the Alaska Statutes, and the section the act added to it, AS 43.20.012, still provides that "the tax imposed by this chapter does not apply to" an individual or a fiduciary.

new-hampshire.name: New Hampshire
new-hampshire._source: New Hampshire does not tax wage income: the NH Dept. of Revenue Administration says the state does not have an income tax on an individual's reported W-2 wages, and its Interest and Dividends Tax was repealed for taxable periods beginning after December 31, 2024. Wages were taxed once, only for nonresidents, by the Commuters Income Tax that Austin v. New Hampshire, 420 U.S. 656 (1975), struck down. https://www.revenue.nh.gov/

_sourceTitles.https://www.revenue.nh.gov/: New Hampshire Department of Revenue Administration

_noTaxBasis.heading: New Hampshire's interest and dividends tax never reached wages, and it ended with 2024
paragraphs: New Hampshire's Interest and Dividends Tax was a tax on investment income rather than on work. It sat in RSA chapter 77, titled "Taxation of Incomes", and the New Hampshire Department of Revenue Administration describes it as "a tax assessed on interest and dividend income." The Department is explicit about pay: the state "does not have an income tax on an individual's reported W-2 wages."

That tax is now gone as well. The Department records that it was assessed at 5% for tax periods ending before 31 December 2023, at 4% for periods ending on or after that date, and at 3% for periods ending on or after 31 December 2024, and that it "was repealed for taxable periods beginning after December 31, 2024." The legislature's text of chapter 77 now reads only that the entire chapter was repealed by a 2021 act, effective 1 January 2025.

New Hampshire has taxed wages before, but only the wages of people living in other states. The Commuters Income Tax took 4% of a nonresident's New Hampshire-derived income above a $2,000 exemption, and employers had to withhold it. On 19 March 1975, in Austin v. New Hampshire, the U.S. Supreme Court held that the tax violates the Privileges and Immunities Clause, because it fell exclusively on nonresidents' incomes.

For a salaried employee the 2025 repeal changed nothing on the pay stub, because wages sat outside the tax throughout. It matters to a resident with savings or a brokerage account, who no longer owes the Interest and Dividends Tax for taxable periods beginning in 2025 or later. On a New Hampshire salary anywhere on this ladder, each dollar withheld goes to federal tax, Social Security or Medicare.

overtimePremiumDeduction.label: Overtime exclusion
overtimePremiumDeduction._source: HB 463 (2026, as passed House and Senate, HB 463/AP; signed May 11, 2026), section 2-4, adds O.C.G.A. 48-7-27(a)(16): 'For all taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, and ending on December 31, 2028, any amount of qualified overtime compensation, as such term is defined in Section 225 of the Internal Revenue Code, up to $1,750.00 received by a full-time employee paid by an hourly wage.' It is one of the amounts subtracted from federal adjusted gross income to reach Georgia taxable net income (48-7-27(a): 'the taxpayer's federal adjusted gross income ... less'). 26 U.S.C. 225 counts only the overtime pay in excess of the regular rate, so only the premium counts, and it has no income limit of its own. Employers report the amounts to the Department (48-7-27(a)(16)(C)); nothing in the act changes withholding, so it is left out of withholding here. The cap reads per employee, so on a joint return each spouse's own overtime counts toward that spouse's $1,750. Salaried employees do not qualify, whatever their overtime. https://www.legis.ga.gov/api/legislation/document/20252026/249080

cashTipsDeduction.label: Cash tips exclusion
cashTipsDeduction._source: HB 463 (2026, as passed House and Senate, HB 463/AP; signed May 11, 2026), section 2-4, adds O.C.G.A. 48-7-27(a)(17): 'For all taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, any amount up to $1,750.00 received in cash tips.' 'Cash tips' means cash received by an individual in an occupation that customarily and regularly receives tips, including tips paid in cash or charged and tips received under a tip-sharing arrangement, if paid voluntarily, not negotiated and set by the payor; the occupation must have a Treasury Tipped Occupation Code, and occupations excluded under IRC 63 are excluded here too ((17)(D)). The paragraph is repealed December 31, 2028 ((17)(E)). It has no income limit and is not tied to the federal deduction, so it is the tips themselves up to $1,750, even where the federal deduction phases out. https://www.legis.ga.gov/api/legislation/document/20252026/249080

ficaPaidDeduction._statute: M.G.L. c.62 s.3(B)(a)(3), read verbatim on 2026-08-02: 'Taxes paid to the United States under the provisions of the Federal Insurance Contributions Act or the Federal Railroad Retirement Act. In no event shall the aggregate of the otherwise allowable deductions of this subparagraph and of all sums deducted from wages as contributions to an annuity, pension, endowment or retirement fund of the United States government, the commonwealth or any political subdivision thereof, attributable to any one taxpayer exceed two thousand dollars.' The $2,000 cap is a fixed statutory figure, not inflation-indexed.
ficaPaidDeduction._crosscheck: MA DOR, 2025 Form 1 instructions, 'Line 11. Amount Paid to Social Security and Medicare (FICA), Railroad, U.S. or Massachusetts Retirement Systems': 'If you have paid into any of the retirement systems listed above during 2025, you may deduct those contributions, up to a maximum of $2,000. Enter in lines 11a and 11b the amount you, and your spouse if filing jointly, paid to Social Security (FICA), Medicare or Railroad Retirement and the U.S. or Massachusetts retirement systems during 2025 as shown on your Form W-2, but not more than $2,000 each. Payment amounts may not be combined or transferred from one spouse to the other. Be sure to add any amount of Medicare tax withheld as shown on Form W-2.' That settles three things: the deduction is the FICA the employee actually paid rather than a flat $2,000, Medicare counts toward it, and the cap is per person with no pooling between spouses. maryland.name: Maryland
maryland._source: Maryland tax year 2026. RATES AND BRACKETS are current for 2026: the Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act of 2025 (House Bill 352, Chapter 604, approved 2025-05-20) set the schedule that applies to tax years beginning after 2024-12-31, keeping the 2% to 5.75% ladder and adding two high-income brackets, 6.25% and 6.5%. Maryland's bracket thresholds are fixed in statute and are not inflation-indexed, so 2026 uses the same thresholds. STANDARD DEDUCTION is the tax year 2025 amount, not a 2026 amount. The same Act rewrote Md. Code, Tax-General 10-217 into flat dollar amounts, $3,350 for a single filer, married filing separately, or a dependent, and $6,700 for a head of household, a qualifying surviving spouse, or a joint return, and it repealed the older rule that set the deduction at 15% of Maryland adjusted gross income between a floor and a ceiling. Section 10-217(c) then requires a cost-of-living adjustment for each tax year beginning after 2025-12-31, determined by the Comptroller, with the increase rounded down to the next lowest multiple of $50. So a 2026 amount exists in law, but Maryland has not published it: the Department of Legislative Services fiscal note for House Bill 411 of the 2026 session (First Reader, 2026-02-11) states that the 2026 amounts have not yet been announced, House Bill 411 itself died in committee, and the Comptroller has issued no 2026 figure since. This page therefore subtracts the 2025 statutory amounts and says so on the page. ABOUT $3,400, which is easy to mistake for the 2026 answer: the 2026 Maryland Employer Withholding Guide says that for the purpose of the percentage method calculation the Standard Deduction is $3,400, but that is an input an employer uses to work out withholding from a paycheck, and the guide prints that one figure above both of its rate tables, the joint and head of household table and the single table. The statute is not status-blind, it gives $3,350 to a single filer and $6,700 to a joint filer, so one all-status $3,400 cannot be the statutory per-status amount. Raising the single filer to $3,400 while leaving a joint filer at $6,700 would also apply the cost-of-living adjustment to one filing status only, which section 10-217(c) does not do. Head of household uses the joint bracket thresholds and the $6,700 deduction. Sources: Md. Code, Tax-General 10-217, https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gtg&section=10-217 ; House Bill 352 of 2025 as enrolled (Chapter 604), https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/2025RS/bills/hb/hb0352e.pdf ; fiscal note for House Bill 411 of 2026, https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/2026RS/fnotes/bil_0001/hb0411.pdf ; Comptroller of Maryland tax alert on the 2025 session changes to standard and itemized deductions, https://www.marylandcomptroller.gov/content/dam/mdcomp/tax/legal-publications/alerts/tax-alert-changes-to-standard-and-itemized-deductions-and-to-state-and-local-income-tax-rates-from-the-2025-legislative-session.pdf ; 2026 Maryland Employer Withholding Guide, https://www.marylandcomptroller.gov/content/dam/mdcomp/tax/instructions/withholding/2026/withholding-guide.pdf

Graduated 4-bracket schedule (3.5%/4.4%/5.3%/7.65%), inflation-indexed and officially PUBLISHED for tax year 2026. Schedule B (Married Filing Jointly): 3.5% to $20,150, 4.4% to $69,260, 5.3% to $443,630, 7.65% above. STANDARD DEDUCTION, added 2026-08-02: the same official page prints the 2026 Standard Deduction schedules, and Wisconsin's deduction slides down with income rather than being a flat amount (Wis. Stat. 71.05(22)(dp)). Single: '$0 to $20,119 → $13,960' then '20,119 to 136,453 → 13,960 less 12% ... $20,120' then '136,453 → 0'. Married filing jointly: '$0 to $29,039 → $25,840' then '29,039 to 159,690 → 25,840 less 19.778% $29,040' then '159,690 → 0'. Head of household: '$0 to $20,119 → $18,030', then '20,119 to 58,827 → 18,030 less 22.515% $20,120', then '58,827 to 136,453 → 13,960 less 12% ... 20,120', then '136,453 → 0'. HOW IT IS ENCODED: the engine's standardDeductionPhaseout is one straight line per status (reduction = floor(base x excess / denominator)), so 'reduce by R% of the excess' is written as denominator = base / R. Single: 13,960 / 0.12 = 116,333.33, which puts the zero point at 20,120 + 116,333.33 = 136,453.33, matching the schedule's own 136,453 cutoff; at $75,000 it gives a $7,375 deduction against the statute's $7,374.40, the whole gap being the engine rounding the reduction down to a whole dollar. Married: 25,840 / 0.19778 = 130,650.22, zero at 29,040 + 130,650.22 = 159,690.22, matching 159,690; at $75,000 it gives $16,751 against the statute's $16,750.03. HEAD OF HOUSEHOLD IS AN APPROXIMATION, disclosed to readers: Wisconsin's head-of-household schedule bends twice, and the engine's single straight line cannot express that, so we use the schedule's own second segment (13,960 less 12% over $20,120). That is EXACT for Wisconsin income of $58,827 and above, including the $75,000 benchmark, and it understates the deduction below $58,827, where the statute allows up to $18,030, so head-of-household tax runs high there by at most about $140 a year. https://www.revenue.wi.gov/TaxForms2026/2026-Form1-ES-Inst.pdf

steppedRecapture._statute: Conn. Gen. Stat. 12-700(a)(10), subparagraphs (A)(ii) unmarried, (B)(ii) head of household, (C)(ii) married filing jointly. Read verbatim from cga.ct.gov on 2026-08-02. (A)(ii): 'Notwithstanding the provisions of subparagraph (A)(i) of this subdivision, for each taxpayer whose Connecticut adjusted gross income exceeds fifty-six thousand five hundred dollars, the amount of the taxpayer's Connecticut taxable income to which the two-per-cent tax rate applies shall be reduced by one thousand dollars for each five thousand dollars, or fraction thereof, by which the taxpayer's Connecticut adjusted gross income exceeds said amount. Any such amount of Connecticut taxable income to which, as provided in the preceding sentence, the two-per-cent tax rate does not apply shall be an amount to which the four-and-one-half-per-cent tax rate shall apply.' (B)(ii) is the same sentence with 'seventy-eight thousand five hundred dollars' and 'one thousand six hundred dollars for each four thousand dollars'. (C)(ii) is the same sentence with 'one hundred thousand five hundred dollars' and 'two thousand dollars for each five thousand dollars'.
steppedRecapture._derivation: Moving income from the 2.0% band to the 4.5% band costs the 2.5-point difference, so amountPerStep = (income moved per step) x 0.025: single 1,000 x 0.025 = 25, head of household 1,600 x 0.025 = 40, married jointly 2,000 x 0.025 = 50. The ceiling is the width of the 2% band, which can only be emptied once: single 10,000 x 0.025 = 250, head of household 16,000 x 0.025 = 400, married jointly 20,000 x 0.025 = 500, each reached after ten steps.
steppedRecapture._crosscheck: DRS IP 2026(7) page 9, 'Table C - 2% Tax Rate Phase-Out Add-Back', reproduces all three ladders row for row. Single is the Withholding Code F column ($0 up to $56,500; $56,500-$61,500 = $25; then $25 more every $5,000; '$101,500 and up' = $250). Head of household is Code B ($0 up to $78,500; then $40 every $4,000; '$114,500 and up' = $400). Married filing jointly is Code C ($0 up to $100,500; then $50 every $5,000; '$145,500 and up' = $500). Withholding Code A is MARRIED FILING SEPARATELY, not single: Table A on page 7 gives Code A a $12,000 personal exemption, which 12-702 assigns to a married individual filing separately, and gives Code F $15,000, the unmarried amount. Statute 12-700(a)(10)(D)(ii) confirms the separate ladder ($50,250 threshold, $1,000 moved per $2,500). Reading Code A as single would overcharge a $75,000 single filer by $150.

Rates are statutory (Conn. Gen. Stat. ch. 229), NOT inflation-indexed, and unchanged for 2026 (the 2024 cut of the lowest two rates to 2%/4.5% is fully phased in). Single=Code F, MFS=Code A, HoH=Code B, MFJ=Code C; codes A, D and F share one Table B schedule, which is why the single/MFS mix-up in an earlier draft of this note did not move the bracket figures, but it WOULD move Table C, so the mapping is now stated the way Table A's personal exemptions prove it ($12,000 under Code A is the 12-702 married-filing-separately amount, $15,000 under Code F is the unmarried amount). (1) The personal-exemption amounts had lost their leading digits and rendered to readers as bare ',000'. They are restored from Conn. Gen. Stat. 12-702, which sets the exemption at 'twelve thousand dollars' for a married individual filing separately (phasing out above $24,000 of Connecticut AGI), 'fifteen thousand dollars' for an unmarried individual for taxable years commencing on or after January 1, 2016 (phasing out above $30,000), 'nineteen thousand dollars' for a head of household (above $38,000), and $24,000 for a joint return (above $48,000). Note the earlier draft of this fix had single and married-filing-separately swapped; the statute settles it, single is $15,000. (2) The phase-out add-back was called the '3%' phase-out and described as hitting only high earners. Since tax year 2024 it is the 2% phase-out: Conn. Gen. disclaimer: Connecticut has no local/municipal income tax.

Connecticut has no standard deduction. It gives a personal exemption instead: up to $15,000 if you are single, $24,000 married filing jointly, $19,000 head of household, and $12,000 married filing separately. The exemption shrinks by $1,000 for every $1,000 of Connecticut income above $30,000 single, $48,000 jointly, $38,000 head of household and $24,000 filing separately, so it runs out entirely a little way above those points. Neither the exemption nor Connecticut's personal tax credits are modeled here, so this estimate runs HIGH for lower incomes.

Connecticut's 2% tax-rate phase-out (the Table C add-back) IS now included in the figures above, and it is not just a high-earner rule. For a single filer it starts at $56,500 of Connecticut income and adds $25 for every $5,000 above that, up to $250; head of household starts at $78,500 and adds $40 per $4,000, up to $400; married filing jointly starts at $100,500 and adds $50 per $5,000, up to $500. Any amount over the starting point counts as a full step, so a single filer $1 past $56,500 already pays the first $25. We measure it against your wages only, so if you also have interest, dividends or self-employment income, your real Connecticut income is higher and the add-back could be a step or two bigger. The separate high-income tax recapture (Table D) is still not modeled. If you are married but filing separately, Connecticut starts that add-back earlier than the single ladder used here, at $50,250 in $2,500 steps rather than $56,500 in $5,000 steps, so your real Connecticut tax can run somewhat higher than shown, by up to about $150 from the add-back alone; your personal exemption is smaller too, $12,000 rather than the $15,000 above.
Single bracket key also covers Married Filing Separately (CT Code F uses the same Code A schedule).

missouri._source: Tax year 2026 Missouri brackets and standard deduction come from the Missouri Department of Revenue's 2026 Missouri Withholding Tax Formula and are confirmed by the tax rate chart on the 2026 Form MO-1040ES. Missouri applies one graduated schedule to every filing status: no tax on the first $1,348 of Missouri taxable income, then 2.0%, 2.5%, 3.0%, 3.5%, 4.0% and 4.5% in $1,348 steps, with the top rate of 4.7% on income over $9,436. Only the standard deduction changes with filing status, and for 2026 it matches the federal amounts: $16,100 single or married filing separate, $32,200 married when the spouse does not work, and $24,150 head of household. Separately from withholding, Section 143.171 RSMo still allows Missouri filers to deduct part of their federal income tax on the annual return. The deduction is a percentage of federal income tax liability set by Missouri adjusted gross income (35% at $25,000 or less, 25% from $25,001 to $50,000, 15% from $50,001 to $100,000, 5% from $100,001 to $125,000, 0% at $125,001 or more), capped at $5,000 per return or $10,000 on a married filing combined return, and it is claimed on Form MO-1040. Missouri's withholding formula does not apply it, so it does not change what your employer withholds. This estimate models the annual return, so it applies the deduction (added 2026-10-02). kansas._source: Kansas tax year 2026 individual income tax: two-bracket schedule 5.20% / 5.58% enacted by Senate Bill 1 (June 2024 special session), which consolidated Kansas's prior three brackets (3.10% / 5.25% / 5.70%) into two and lowered the rates to 5.20% (taxable income up to $23,000 single/HoH, $46,000 married filing jointly) and 5.58% on income above those thresholds. Tax Foundation's 2026 state income tax data lists exactly these 2026 rates/thresholds for Kansas, and the standard deduction $3,605 single / $8,240 MFJ (HoH $6,180 per Kansas DOR). These statutory amounts are unchanged for 2026: SB269's conditional phase-down toward 4.0% only triggers if the state budget stabilization fund reaches 15% of the prior year balance, and that trigger did NOT lower the 2026 rates (Tax Foundation still lists 5.20%/5.58% for 2026). RESOLVED a conflict: one secondary source (LegalClarity) claims Kansas uses 3.10%/5.70% for 2026 with $30k/$60k thresholds — those are the PRE-REFORM legacy rates (3.1%/5.7% were the old bottom/top rates) mislabeled as current; rejected in favor of Tax Foundation 2026 + AARP + EY tax-news + WebSearch consensus on 5.20%/5.58%. Head of household uses the single $23,000 threshold with its own $6,180 standard deduction. PERSONAL EXEMPTION CORRECTED 2026-08-02: the disclaimer used to give head-of-household filers the same $9,160 exemption as single filers. K.S.A. 79-32,121b(a)(2) allows '$9,160' to 'all other individuals with a filing status of single, head of household or married filing separate', and then (b)(1) adds: 'Any individual filing a federal income tax return under the status of head of household, as defined in 26 U.S.C. Sec. 2(b), shall be allowed an additional Kansas exemption of $2,320 for tax year 2024 and all tax years thereafter.' Head of household is therefore $11,480. https://www.ksrevisor.gov/statutes/chapters/ch79/079_032_0121b.html PERSONAL EXEMPTION FOLDED IN 2026-10-03: the standard deduction field now carries the standard deduction plus the K.S.A. 79-32,121b personal exemption, $3,605 + $9,160 = $12,765 single, $8,240 + $18,320 = $26,560 married filing jointly, and $6,180 + $9,160 + $2,320 = $17,660 head of household. The statute sets flat amounts with no tax-year limit and no income test: '(1) In the case of married individuals filing a joint return, a personal exemption of $18,320; (2) ... single, head of household or married filing separate, a personal exemption of $9,160'. Dependent exemptions are not modelled.
disclaimer: Kansas has no local/city income tax on wages.

This estimate includes Kansas's personal exemption, added to the standard deduction: $9,160 single, $18,320 married filing jointly and $11,480 head of household, because a head-of-household filer gets an extra $2,320. With the standard deduction ($3,605, $8,240 and $6,180) that comes to $12,765, $26,560 and $17,660. The extra $2,320 exemption for each dependent is not included.
Kansas itemized deductions, tax credits (e.g. food sales tax credit, child/dependent care), and the additional standard deduction for filers age 65+ or blind are not modeled.
kansas.notes: Two-bracket 5.20% / 5.58% (Senate Bill 1, 2024; unchanged for 2026). The amount subtracted is the standard deduction plus the personal exemption. No local income tax.

arkansas.name: Arkansas
arkansas._source: Arkansas individual income tax for tax year 2026. The rates come from Act 1 of the First Extraordinary Session, 2026 (House Bill 1001, approved 5/6/2026), which amended Arkansas Code 26-51-201(a)(4) and lowered the top rate from 3.9% to 3.7% for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026. The statutory schedule is 0% up to $5,599, 2% to $11,199, 3% to $15,999, 3.4% to $26,399, and 3.7% from $26,400 to $94,700, and Arkansas applies the same schedule to every filing status. An identical companion measure, Act 2 of the same session (Senate Bill 1), was approved the same day. The standard deduction of $2,470 per taxpayer comes from the Arkansas Department of Finance and Administration Withholding Tax Formula Method, Tax Year 2026, effective 01/01/2026. Because the rate cut was signed in May 2026, that withholding booklet still prints the older 3.9% rate; the figures shown here follow the statute. Sources: Act 1 at https://www.arkleg.state.ar.us/Home/FTPDocument?path=%2FACTS%2F2026S1%2FPublic%2FACT1.pdf and the DFA 2026 withholding formula at https://www.dfa.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/whformula_2026.pdf RELABELLED 2026-10-03 as 2025 figures (figureYear 2025, scope thresholdsAndDeduction): the bracket thresholds Act 1 prints (5,599 / 11,199 / 15,999 / 26,399, with 94,700 for the top band) are the ones DFA published as its '2025 Indexed Tax Brackets', and Act 1 keeps the rule that 'The tables set forth in subdivisions (a)(1)-(4) of this section shall be adjusted annually'. The $2,470 standard deduction ($4,940 married filing jointly) is the 2025 return amount in the 2025 AR1000F/AR1000NR instructions. DFA has not published 2026 indexed thresholds or a 2026 standard deduction (its 2026 withholding formula still uses $2,470 and the 3.9% rate), so only the 3.7% rate here is a 2026 figure. https://www.dfa.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025_TaxBrackets.pdf ; https://www.dfa.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025_AR1000F_and_AR1000NR_Instructions.pdf

Arkansas gives a $29 personal tax credit for each withholding exemption claimed on Form AR4EC, plus dependent credits. Those are not modeled here, so estimates run slightly high for most filers.

Once net taxable income passes $94,700, Arkansas phases out the benefit of the lower brackets, so the effective rate moves toward a flat 3.7% on all income. That taper is not modeled, so estimates above roughly $95,000 run modestly low.

Arkansas lowered its top rate to 3.7% in May 2026, backdated to January 1, 2026. Withholding tables printed before the cut still use 3.9%, so the tax actually taken out of your paycheck may be a little higher than shown here until your employer updates its tables.

Arkansas's 2026 rates are current, but the bracket thresholds and the $2,470 standard deduction used here are its 2025 inflation-adjusted amounts. Arkansas adjusts them every year and has not yet published its 2026 amounts.
arkansas.notes: Progressive 0% to 3.7% for tax year 2026, on Arkansas's 2025 inflation-adjusted bracket thresholds and standard deduction until it publishes 2026 ones. The top 3.7% rate begins at $26,400 of net taxable income. Arkansas uses the same rate schedule for every filing status; the standard deduction is $2,470 per taxpayer (2025 amount). No local or city income tax.

alabama.name: Alabama

standardDeductionPhaseout._statute: Ala. Code 40-18-15(b)(4), tax years beginning after December 31, 2021; the floor also carries the 40-18-19(a)(8) personal exemption, which does not phase out

federalTaxSubtraction.label: Federal income tax deduction
federalTaxSubtraction._statute: Ala. Code 40-18-15(c); Constitution of Alabama 2022, section 211.04
federalTaxSubtraction._source: Ala. Code 40-18-15(c): 'A deduction is allowable for the amount of federal income tax paid or accrued within the taxable year.' Section 211.04 of the Constitution of Alabama requires it: 'a resident individual taxpayer shall be allowed to deduct from his gross income the amount of federal income tax paid or accrued within the taxable year.' Neither sets a cap. ADOR rule 810-3-15-.20 defines the accrued amount as the federal 'Tax' amount 'less all credits which reduce the amount of the taxpayer's federal income tax liability'. The same rule lets the filer's method decide which amount is deducted: 'A cash basis taxpayer may allocate his federal income tax deduction on the cash basis or accrual basis', while 'An accrual basis taxpayer must allocate his federal income tax deduction using the accrual basis.' (It also records that, under its power to select the method, 'the Department chooses the accrual basis'.) This estimate uses the accrued amount, the year's own federal liability, which is what the 2025 Form 40 Federal Income Tax Deduction Worksheet computes starting from Form 1040 line 22; a cash-basis filer deducting what was paid in the year would get a different figure. Alabama's 2026 withholding formula also subtracts the employee's annual federal withholding. https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/code-of-alabama?section=40-18-15 ; https://admincode.legislature.state.al.us/administrative-code/810-3-15-.20 ; https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/25f40bk.pdf

overtimePremiumDeduction.label: Overtime premium deduction
overtimePremiumDeduction._statute: Ala. Code 40-18-15(a)(29), added by Act 2026-604 (HB527, 2026 Regular Session)
overtimePremiumDeduction._source: Act 2026-604 (HB527 of the 2026 Regular Session, signed April 16, 2026) adds subdivision (a)(29) to Ala. Code 40-18-15: 'For tax years beginning on and after January 1, 2026, and ending December 31, 2028, qualified overtime compensation received during the taxable year, not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) per taxpayer. For purposes of this deduction, qualified overtime compensation shall be defined and calculated pursuant to the provisions of 26 U.S.C. § 225. An individual taxpayer shall be allowed the deduction for qualified overtime compensation, regardless of whether the taxpayer itemizes income tax deductions in calculating the income tax imposed pursuant to Section 40-18-5.' Section 3 of the act makes that section of the Code effective October 1, 2026, and the deduction it adds covers tax years 2026 through 2028; the Alabama Department of Revenue applies it 'Beginning with the 2026 and ending with the 2028 calendar year'. 26 U.S.C. § 225(c)(1) defines qualified overtime compensation as overtime pay required by section 7 of the Fair Labor Standards Act 'that is in excess of the regular rate', so only the premium counts, the extra half in time and a half. The Alabama Department of Revenue says the same: 'The deduction is the lesser of the actual overtime premium or a maximum annual amount of $1,000 per taxpayer', and it gives no income limit. It is a deduction on the Alabama return, not an exclusion from wages: the premium is reported in Form W-2 box 12 code TT, and the Department says that entry 'will not change wages, withholdings, or taxes on Form W2', so it is left out of withholding here. Because subdivision (a)(29) is a deduction under subsection (a), it does not lower Alabama adjusted gross income, so the standard deduction chart is still read at the income before it. The cap is applied to one earner's own overtime; the act's 'per taxpayer' wording is not tested here for a couple who both work overtime. https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/files/pdf/SearchableInstruments/2026RS/HB527-enr.pdf ; https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/individual-corporate/overtime-premium-deduction-act-2026-604/ ; https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/225

alabama._source: Alabama individual income tax: statutory three-bracket schedule 2%/4%/5% under Ala. Code § 40-18-5, unchanged for 2026, so figureYear=2026. Single/MFS/HoH thresholds: 2% to $500, 4% to $3,000, 5% above. Married-filing-jointly thresholds (exactly 2x single): 2% to $1,000, 4% to $6,000, 5% above. Confirmed across Tax Foundation 2026, halfpricesoft 2026, icalculator 2026, and AARP 2026 (identical brackets). STANDARD DEDUCTION, income-phased since 2026-10-02 per Ala. Code § 40-18-15(b)(4) and the ADOR Standard Deduction Chart (Form 40 booklet, page 9): below $25,500 of Alabama AGI it is $3,000 single, $8,500 married filing jointly and $5,200 head of family; each full $500 of AGI over $25,500 takes off $25 single, $175 married or $135 head of family; and it never falls below $2,500 single, $5,000 married or $2,500 head of family, which every status reaches at $35,500. FEDERAL INCOME TAX DEDUCTION, applied since 2026-10-02 per Ala. Code § 40-18-15(c), in full with no cap. Hand-verified single $75,000: standard deduction $2,500 (at its floor), federal income tax $7,670, taxable 75,000 - 2,500 - 7,670 = 64,830, tax = 2% x 500 + 4% x 2,500 + 5% x 61,830 = $3,201.50. OVERTIME PREMIUM DEDUCTION, modeled at filing since 2026-10-02 per Ala. Code § 40-18-15(a)(29) as added by Act 2026-604 (HB527, 2026 Regular Session): the overtime premium (the pay above the regular rate, as 26 U.S.C. § 225 defines it), up to $1,000 a year, tax years 2026 through 2028, with no income limit, claimed on the return and not in withholding. https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/state-income-tax-rates-2026/ ; https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/forms/standard-deduction-chart-40-3/ ; https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/code-of-alabama?section=40-18-15 ; https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/files/pdf/SearchableInstruments/2026RS/HB527-enr.pdf ; https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/individual-corporate/overtime-premium-deduction-act-2026-604/ PERSONAL EXEMPTION FOLDED IN 2026-10-03: Ala. Code 40-18-19(a)(8) allows 'in the case of a head of a family or a married person living with husband or wife, a personal exemption of three thousand dollars ($3,000)' and $1,500 for a single person, with no income condition; the 2025 Form 40 booklet says 'If you check box 1, enter $1,500 on line 13' and 'If you check box 2, enter $3,000 on line 13'. The standard deduction field and the phase-out floors therefore carry it: 3,000 + 1,500 = 4,500 single (floor 2,500 + 1,500 = 4,000), 8,500 + 3,000 = 11,500 married filing jointly (floor 8,000), 5,200 + 3,000 = 8,200 head of family (floor 5,500). The steps are unchanged because only the standard deduction steps down. The dependent exemption, 40-18-19(a)(9), is not modelled. https://alisondb.legislature.state.al.us/alison/CodeOfAlabama/1975/40-18-19.htm ; https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/25f40bk.pdf
disclaimer: Alabama's standard deduction shrinks as income rises, and this estimate follows Alabama's own chart: a single filer gets $3,000, reduced by $25 for each full $500 of Alabama adjusted gross income over $25,500, and $2,500 from $35,500 up. Married filing jointly goes from $8,500 down to $5,000, and head of family from $5,200 down to $2,500, over the same income range.

This estimate also includes Alabama's personal exemption, which does not shrink with income: $1,500 single, $3,000 married filing jointly and $3,000 head of family. The amounts shown combine it with the standard deduction, so a single filer's goes from $4,500 down to $4,000. The dependent exemption is not modeled.

Local income taxes are not included. Many Alabama municipalities/counties levy a separate LOCAL occupational (wage) tax (e.g. ~1% in Birmingham, Gadsden, Macon County) that is not included in this estimate.

Alabama lets you deduct all of the federal income tax you owe, with no cap, and this estimate applies it. It uses the federal income tax this estimate works out from your pay, so other income or credits on your real return would change it.

The Alabama tax in this estimate does not include Alabama's 2026 overtime deduction, because you claim it on your Alabama return when you file and it does not change what comes out of your paychecks. It lets you deduct the extra part of your overtime pay above your normal rate (the "half" in time and a half), up to $1,000 a year. The overtime question on the Alabama paycheck calculator works out what it saves you at filing.
alabama.notes: Progressive 2%-5% (statutory, Ala. Code § 40-18-5), top 5% rate begins at just $3,000 taxable income (single) / $6,000 (married). Standard deduction phases down with income per the ADOR chart, and the full federal income tax deduction is applied. Separate local occupational taxes apply in some cities.

_watch.what: South Carolina's 5.21% top rate can fall automatically from tax year 2027. H.4216 (Act 110 of 2026) writes into S.C. Code 12-6-510: 'beginning with Tax Year 2027 and each year thereafter, the top marginal income tax rate set forth in item (1) must be decreased if individual income tax revenues collected pursuant to this chapter, minus amounts credited to the Trust Fund for Tax Relief, are projected to increase by at least five percent in the fiscal year that begins during the tax year', and 'The reduction required by this item shall continue until the top marginal income tax rate equals 1.99 percent.' The size of the cut is set by the Board of Economic Advisors, and item (4) fixes the deadline: 'the forecast in effect on February fifteenth of the current fiscal year is the final forecast for which the percentage adjustment is determined.' Re-verify after 15 February 2027: was a 2027 rate below 5.21% certified? Source: https://www.scstatehouse.gov/sess126_2025-2026/bills/4216.htm
_watch.decided: Audit 2026-08-02: the trigger cannot move the tax-year-2026 rates, which are the ones encoded here.

south-carolina._source: South Carolina individual income tax — OFFICIAL South Carolina Dept. of Revenue guidance on H.4216 (Act 110, signed March 30, 2026), EFFECTIVE for tax year 2026 (returns due April 15, 2027). H.4216 REPLACES SC's old 0%/3%/6% three-bracket system entirely for TY2026 with a two-rate schedule on federal-AGI-based taxable income: 'the tax rate for income less than $30,000 is 1.99%' and 'the tax rate for income from $30,000 and above is 5.21%, minus $966.' The '5.21% minus $966' form is mathematically identical to a marginal two-bracket schedule (verified continuity at $30,000: 1.99% x 30000 = $597 = 5.21% x 30000 - 966), so modeled as marginal brackets: 1.99% to $30,000, 5.21% above — SAME rates for all filing statuses. SCDOR also created the new SC Income-Adjusted Deduction (SCIAD) replacing the federal standard/itemized deduction: $15,000 single/MFS, $22,500 head of household, $30,000 MFJ/surviving spouse (modeled as the standardDeduction). RESOLVED A GENUINE SOURCE CONFLICT: the Tax Foundation 2026 dataset still lists SC's OLD 0%/3%/6% system (top reverting to 6.2% on 7/1/2026) and federal std deduction $8,350/$16,700 — it predates H.4216, which was signed only March 30, 2026. The official SCDOR H.4216 page (ranked first per loop procedure) overrides the stale secondary, and PolicyEngine + ITEP corroborate the 1.99%/5.21% + SCIAD structure. figureYear=2026 (genuine official 2026 data, no prior-year fallback). WORKED EXAMPLE, recomputed 2026-08-02. This field used to record $2,160.00 for a single filer at $75,000, which was measured before the SCIAD phase-down was encoded and no longer matches what the calculator returns. Redone from the data in this file: the reduction is floor(15,000 x (75,000 - 40,000) / 55,000) rounded down to the next lowest ten dollars = floor(9,545.45) -> $9,540, so the SCIAD is 15,000 - 9,540 = $5,460 and taxable income is 75,000 - 5,460 = $69,540. Tax = 1.99% x 30,000 + 5.21% x 39,540 = 597.00 + 2,060.03 = $2,657.03, which is what the calculator now shows. https://dor.sc.gov/news/information-about-h-4216 ; https://www.policyengine.org/us/south-carolina-2026-tax-changes

_sourceTitles.https://dor.sc.gov/news/information-abou: South Carolina Department of Revenue: information about H.4216

disclaimer: South Carolina rewrote its income tax for 2026 (H. 4216, Act 110): 1.99% on taxable income below $30,000 and 5.21% above, with the South Carolina Income Adjusted Deduction (SCIAD) replacing the federal standard deduction. The SCIAD starts at $15,000 for single or married filing separately, $22,500 for head of household and $30,000 for married filing jointly, and shrinks as income rises until it reaches zero at $95,000, $142,500 and $190,000 respectively. This calculator now applies that reduction. The statute measures it against your federal adjusted gross income; we use your wages less pre-tax deductions, so if you have income or adjustments outside your paycheck your real deduction may be smaller than shown.

South Carolina starts from federal AGI; this estimate approximates taxable income as wages minus the SCIAD and does not model federal-AGI adjustments, the capped state EITC ($200), or other SC credits.
South Carolina has no local/city income tax on wages.
Under H.4216 the top rate may be reduced further in future years if state revenue triggers are met; figures shown are the enacted 2026 rates.

Paycheck withholding is a separate calculation from the yearly tax. The 2026 SC Withholding Tax Formula the SC Department of Revenue currently publishes (form WH-1603F, Rev. 11/4/25) was issued before H. 4216 was signed and still withholds at the older 0%, 3% and 6% rates using a $5,000 personal allowance. Until the SCDOR reissues it, the South Carolina tax withheld on a 2026 paystub may not match the yearly estimate shown here.
south-carolina.notes: Two-rate 1.99% / 5.21% (H.4216 / Act 110, new for tax year 2026), 5.21% begins above $30,000 taxable income. New SC Income-Adjusted Deduction (SCIAD) replaces the federal standard deduction; it phases down with income. No local income tax.

Three statutory rates 5.8% / 6.75% / 7.15%, PLUS a NEW 2% surcharge (effective for tax years beginning on/after Jan 1, 2026) on Maine taxable income over $1,000,000 single / $1,500,000 MFJ and HoH / $750,000 MFS — modeled as a fourth marginal band at 9.15% (= 7.15% + 2%) beginning at those thresholds. Single/MFS: 5.8% to $27,400, 6.75% to $64,850, 7.15% to $1,000,000, 9.15% above. MFJ/surviving spouse: 5.8% to $54,850, 6.75% to $129,750, 7.15% to $1,500,000, 9.15% above. HoH: 5.8% to $41,100, 6.75% to $97,300, 7.15% to $1,500,000, 9.15% above (our 'single' key uses the SINGLE $1,000,000 surcharge threshold; MFS filers reach the surcharge at $750,000, which is disclaimed). 2026 standard deduction (official MRS schedule): $15,700 single/MFS, $31,400 MFJ, $23,550 HoH. RESOLVED a source conflict: Tax Foundation 2026 lists Maine's standard deduction as $8,350/$16,700 — those are Maine's lower phase-out FLOOR amounts, NOT the base 2026 standard deduction; the official MRS 2026 schedule ($15,700/$31,400/$23,550) ranks first and is used. Tax Foundation otherwise CONFIRMS the 5.8/6.75/7.15% rates and identical bracket thresholds ($27,400/$64,850 single; $54,850/$129,750 MFJ). SIMPLIFICATIONS (disclaimed, state-only): the age/blindness additional deduction and Maine credits are not modeled. No Maine local/city income tax. Hand-verified single $75k -> $3,742.45 (taxable = 75000-15700 = 59300; = 5.8% x 27400 + 6.75% x (59300-27400) = 1589.20 + 2153.25), engine returned 3742.45. SOURCE URL REPLACED 2026-08-02: the previously cited inline-files/ind_tax_rate_sched_2026.pdf returns HTTP 404 and named a superseded revision. The live file is files/2026-05/ind_tax_rate_sched_2026_rev.pdf, headed 'State of Maine 2026 Individual Income Tax Rates' and footed 'Prepared by Maine Revenue Services, Income/Estate Tax Division, Revised: May 20, 2026'. It confirms every figure encoded here: single/MFS 5.8% to $27,400 then 6.75% to $64,850 then 7.15%; head of household $41,100 and $97,300; married filing jointly $54,850 and $129,750; 'Standard Deduction: Single - $15,700, Married Filing Jointly - $31,400, Head of Household - $23,550, Married Filing Separately - $15,700'; 'Personal Exemption: $5,300'; and Note (1), 'For tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, the tax calculated above is increased by a surcharge of 2% on the portion of the taxpayer's Maine taxable income greater than $1,000,000 if filing single, $750,000 if married filing separate; or $1,500,000 if married filing jointly or head of household.' https://www.maine.gov/revenue/sites/maine.gov.revenue/files/2026-05/ind_tax_rate_sched_2026_rev.pdf PERSONAL EXEMPTION AND BOTH PHASE-OUTS MODELLED 2026-10-03: the standard deduction field now carries the standard deduction plus the $5,300 personal exemption ('Personal Exemption: $5,300 - applicable to the taxpayer (and spouse if married filing jointly)', rate schedule above): 21,000 / 42,000 / 28,850. Each part phases out on its own straight line, read from the 2026 estimated tax worksheets (revised December 2025). Standard deduction, 36 M.R.S. 5124-C(2), 'Phaseout of Itemized / Standard Deductions Worksheet' line 6a: starts above '$102,250 if single or married filing separately; $153,400 if head of household; or $204,550 if married filing jointly', over a range of $75,000 / $112,500 / $150,000. Personal exemption, 36 M.R.S. 5126-A, 'Personal Exemption Phaseout Worksheet': starts above '$341,000 if single; $375,050 if head of household; $409,150 if married filing jointly', over $125,000 ('the denominator is $62,500 in the case of a married individual filing a separate return and $125,000 in all other cases'). The worksheets round the fraction to four decimals; the engine floors the reduction to whole dollars instead, a difference of a few dollars at most. https://www.maine.gov/revenue/sites/maine.gov.revenue/files/inline-files/26_item_stand_%20ded_phaseout_wksht_0.pdf ; https://www.maine.gov/revenue/sites/maine.gov.revenue/files/inline-files/26_1040es_pers_exempt_phaseout_wksht.pdf
disclaimer: This estimate includes Maine's $5,300 personal exemption ($10,600 for a married couple filing jointly), added to the standard deduction. Both shrink at higher incomes and both reductions are applied: for a single filer the $15,700 standard deduction shrinks away between $102,250 and $177,250 of income, and the exemption between $341,000 and $466,000. Maine rounds the share it takes away slightly differently, so the result can differ from your return by a few dollars.

For 2026 Maine adds a 2% surcharge on taxable income above $1,000,000 (single), $1,500,000 (married filing jointly / head of household), or $750,000 (married filing separately). This estimate models the single/joint thresholds; married-filing-separately filers reach the surcharge sooner.
The age-65+/blindness additional deduction and Maine tax credits are not modeled.
Maine has no local or city income tax on wages.
maine.notes: Graduated 5.8% / 6.75% / 7.15% (2026, inflation-indexed), with a new 2% surcharge above $1M (single) / $1.5M (married, head of household) shown as a 9.15% top band. Standard deduction $15,700 single / $31,400 married / $23,550 head of household plus the $5,300 personal exemption ($10,600 married); both phase out at higher incomes. No local income tax.

_watch.what: Hawaii re-conformed to the federal code for tax year 2026, and part of that lands on wages this calculator cannot yet see. Department of Taxation Announcement No. 2026-06 (31 July 2026): 'Act 35 (House Bill 2329, H.D.1, S.D.1, C.D.1) amends section 235-2.3(a), HRS, to conform Hawai'i income tax law to the operative sections of subtitle A, chapter 1, of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC), as amended as of December 31, 2025', in response to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and it 'became effective on May 26, 2026, and applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025'. Hawaii conforms to 'IRC section 224, which creates a deduction of up to $25,000 for qualified tips' but does NOT conform to 'IRC section 225, which creates a deduction of up to $12,500 for qualified overtime compensation' or to the $10,000 vehicle-loan-interest deduction. The engine has no tips or overtime input, so the tips deduction is unmodelled and Hawaii tax runs high for tipped workers. Re-verify when DOTAX publishes its next annual session-law announcement: did the 2027 legislature change conformity, and does the engine now take tip income? Source: https://files.hawaii.gov/tax/news/announce/ann26-06.pdf

hawaii._source: Hawaii individual income tax — OFFICIAL Hawaii Dept. of Taxation Tax Rate Schedules 'For Taxable Years Beginning After December 31, 2024' (tax.hawaii.gov/forms/d_25table-on, the Schedule I/II/III rate schedules from the 2025 N-11 tables packet) for the brackets, PLUS official DOTAX Announcement No. 2025-07 (Dec 1, 2025) for the 2026 standard deduction. GENUINE 2026 data (figureYear=2026, no fallback): Act 46 (SLH 2024) WIDENED Hawaii's 12 brackets for tax year 2025 and RAISES the standard deduction again for tax year 2026; Ann. 2025-07 confirms Act 46 changes nothing else to the bracket schedule for 2026, so the post-2024 widened schedule IS the valid 2026 bracket schedule and the 2026 standard deduction is $8,000 single/MFS, $16,000 MFJ/surviving spouse, $12,000 HoH. Twelve statutory rates 1.4/3.2/5.5/6.4/6.8/7.2/7.6/7.9/8.25/9/10/11%. Schedule I (single/MFS) thresholds 9600/14400/19200/24000/36000/48000/125000/175000/225000/275000/325000. Schedule II (MFJ/surviving spouse) = 2x single: 19200/28800/38400/48000/72000/96000/250000/350000/450000/550000/650000. Schedule III (HoH) = 1.5x single: 14400/21600/28800/36000/54000/72000/187500/262500/337500/412500/487500. All three extracted verbatim from the official DOTAX rate-schedule page (each band's base-dollar amount reconciles to the marginal sum). SIMPLIFICATIONS (disclaimed, state-only): dependent exemptions, the extra exemption for age 65+, itemized deductions, and credits (food/excise tax credit, EITC, child & dependent care) are not modeled. No Hawaii local/county income tax. Hand-verified single $75k -> $3,983.20 (taxable = 75000-8000 = 67000; exact marginal sum of Schedule I lower bands = $2,539.20 + 7.6% x (67000-48000) = 2539.20 + 1444.00; the DOTAX schedule's rounded '$2,539' base differs by $0.20, expected — the engine uses exact marginal math; engine returned 3983.20). https://tax.hawaii.gov/forms/d_25table-on/d_25table-on_p13/ ; https://files.hawaii.gov/tax/news/announce/ann25-07.pdf PERSONAL EXEMPTION FOLDED IN 2026-10-03: HRS 235-54 allows an exemption for each exemption the filer can claim under the Internal Revenue Code and says to 'multiply that number by $1,144, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1984'; the 2025 Form N-11 instructions say 'Multiply $1,144 by the total number of exemptions claimed on line 6e'. One exemption for a single or head-of-household filer and two for a married couple filing jointly gives 9,144 / 18,288 / 13,144. https://www.capitol.hawaii.gov/hrscurrent/Vol04_Ch0201-0257/HRS0235/HRS_0235-0054.htm ; https://files.hawaii.gov/tax/forms/2025/n11_i.pdf
disclaimer: This estimate includes Hawaii's $1,144 personal exemption, added to the standard deduction: one for a single or head-of-household filer and two for a married couple filing jointly. The exemption for each dependent, the extra exemption for filers 65 or older, itemized deductions, and tax credits (the refundable food/excise tax credit, state EITC, and child & dependent care credit) are not modeled, so actual tax for many filers is lower than shown.
Hawaii's standard deduction rose for 2026 under Act 46 to $8,000 single / $16,000 married / $12,000 head of household; the 12-bracket rate schedule is unchanged from 2025.
Hawaii has no local or county income tax on wages.
hawaii.notes: Twelve graduated brackets 1.4%–11% (Act 46 widened schedule, unchanged for 2026). 2026 standard deduction (raised by Act 46): $8,000 single / $16,000 married / $12,000 head of household. No local income tax.

rhode-island._source: Rhode Island individual income tax — 2026 inflation-adjusted figures. RI is a three-bracket graduated state (3.75% / 4.75% / 5.99%) with the SAME bracket schedule for ALL filing statuses (only the standard deduction varies); brackets are inflation-indexed annually and the 2026 amounts ARE officially published (figureYear=2026, no fallback). The official source is RI Division of Taxation Advisory 2025-22 (ADV 2025-22, issued 11/03/2025, 2026 inflation-adjusted personal income tax amounts) — its PDF on tax.ri.gov is Cloudflare/WAF-protected (HTTP 403 to automated fetch and a 'verify you are human' challenge in-browser, which I did NOT bypass), so the figures were taken from authoritative sources that publish ADV 2025-22 verbatim: the official advisory itself confirms the FIRST bracket reaches $82,050 (3.75%) and the standard-deduction/personal-exemption phase-out begins at MAGI $254,250; Tax Foundation 2026 supplies the full schedule and standard deduction: 3.75% to $82,050, 4.75% to $186,450, 5.99% above; standard deduction $11,200 single, $22,400 MFJ. HEAD-OF-HOUSEHOLD standard deduction ($16,800) is DERIVED from RI's documented statutory structure (HoH = single + half the single-to-MFJ gap = 11,200 + (22,400-11,200)/2), which reproduces RI's published prior-year HoH figure exactly (2024: 10,550 + (21,150-10,550)/2 = 15,850 = the reported 2024 HoH); it is the documented RI pattern, not a fabricated value, and is disclaimed as derived. PHASE-OUT AND EXEMPTION CORRECTED 2026-08-02: this field and the disclaimer carried the tax-year-2025 figures. ADV 2025-22 was reached through the Wayback capture of that same tax.ri.gov PDF (tax.ri.gov sits behind a WAF that refuses automated fetch), read with pdftotext. Its 'Phase-out range for standard deduction, exemption amounts by Tax Year' table prints 2025 '$254,250 to $283,250' against 2026 '$261,000 to $290,800', and directly under it: 'Phaseout increment (amount used in computing phaseout), which was $7,250 for 2025, will be $7,450 for 2026.' Its 'Rhode Island personal and dependency exemption amounts by Tax Year' row prints 2025 '$5,100' against 2026 '$5,250'. The same advisory's standard-deduction table also confirms the amounts already encoded here: single $11,200, married filing jointly $22,400, head of household $16,800, married filing separately $11,200. SIMPLIFICATIONS (disclaimed, state-only): dependency exemptions and RI credits are not modeled. No RI local/city income tax. Hand-verified single $75k -> $2,392.50 exact (taxable = 75000-11200 = 63800; entirely in the 3.75% band = 3.75% x 63800; engine returned 2392.50). PERSONAL EXEMPTION AND PHASE-OUT MODELLED 2026-10-03, and the secondary Bloomberg Tax and Tax Foundation links replaced by the advisory itself (original tax.ri.gov URL below; that host refuses automated fetch, so it was read through its Wayback capture). The standard deduction field now carries the standard deduction plus the 2026 $5,250 exemption ('personal and dependency exemption amounts by Tax Year ... 2026 $5,250'): 16,450 / 32,900 / 22,050. R.I. Gen. Laws 44-30-2.6(c)(3)(B)(III) and (D) reduce both by 'twenty (20) percentage points for each five thousand dollars ($5,000) (or fraction thereof)' of AGI over the threshold, inflation-adjusted under (E); ADV 2025-22 gives the 2026 threshold '$261,000 to $290,800' and says the 'Phaseout increment ... will be $7,450 for 2026'. So each $7,450 step, counting a part step as whole, takes 20% of the combined amount (3,290 / 6,580 / 4,410) and five steps take all of it above $290,800. Head of household is given one exemption, the filer's own. https://tax.ri.gov/sites/g/files/xkgbur541/files/2025-11/ADV_2025_22_Inflation_Adjustments.pdf ; https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE44/44-30/44-I/44-30-2.6.htm
disclaimer: Rhode Island's standard deduction and personal exemptions shrink for higher-income filers, and this estimate applies that. For 2026 they lose 20% for each $7,450 (or part of $7,450) of modified adjusted gross income over $261,000, so above $290,800 you get neither.

The standard deductions used here are Rhode Island's official 2026 amounts: $11,200 single, $22,400 married filing jointly, and $16,800 head of household. All three are printed in the RI Division of Taxation's Advisory ADV 2025-22 (2026 inflation-adjusted personal income tax amounts, issued November 3, 2025).

This estimate includes Rhode Island's $5,250 personal exemption for 2026, added to the standard deduction: one for a single or head-of-household filer and two for a married couple filing jointly. Exemptions for dependents and Rhode Island tax credits (property-tax relief, EITC, child & dependent care) are not modeled.
Rhode Island has no local or city income tax on wages.
rhode-island.notes: Three graduated brackets 3.75% / 4.75% / 5.99% (2026, inflation-indexed), same thresholds for all filing statuses: 3.75% to $82,050, 4.75% to $186,450, 5.99% above. Standard deduction $11,200 single / $22,400 married / $16,800 head of household plus the $5,250 personal exemption ($10,500 married); both phase out between $261,000 and $290,800 of MAGI for 2026. No local income tax.
